newsitem.title: USA: Brooke Group's Liggett not for sale - LeBow.
newsitem.headline: Brooke Group's Liggett not for sale - LeBow.

text.p: Brooke Group Ltd chief executive Bennett LeBow said on Friday that Brooke's Liggett Group was not for sale and would turn a profit in 1997 after breaking ranks with other cigarette makers and settling lawsuits in 22 states.

LeBow, flanked at a news conference by Florida Gov. Lawton Chiles and others suing the tobacco industry, defended his decision to settle, saying it was a prudent business move as well as the "right thing to do."

LeBow denied speculation Liggett had settled to make it more attractive to investors, saying the deal providing immunity from tobacco litigation would not automatically transfer to any purchaser of Liggett.
"The settlement of the lawsuit is not portable to the other company," LeBow said.

Liggett, the maker of Chesterfield and Lark cigarettes, rocked the tobacco industry last month with a settlement with 22 state governments. It agreed to turn over a portion of its profits and curb advertising in exchange for immunity.

As part of the agreement, Liggett turned over internal company documents which Florida and other states hope to use to prove that cigarette makers knew of the addictive quality of cigarettes and hid that fact from consumers.
On Monday, a judge in West Palm Beach is expected to rule on whether the documents fall under the attorney-client privilege that cigarette makers claim.
LeBow said Liggett, by far the smallest of the five top U.S. cigarette makers, with less than two percent of the market, lost money in 1996 but has been profitable at other times.
"Liggett made a lot of money through the years. Last year admittedly it was a loss," he said.

"But this year we are back on track and hopefully will make profits. All this publicity you've seen about Liggett's financial condition relates primarily to a debt issue we have due in 1998," LeBow said.
Brooke Group, which also sells trading cards and other interests, reported a net loss of $24.1 million in 1996 and a net profit of $156.6 milion for 1995.
LeBow is the first tobacco executive to cut a deal with states suing the industry to recoup tax dollars spent paying for smoking related illness.
He said he concluded a year ago that the industry could not continue to fend off increasing litigation in the continuing battle over product liability.
"Liggett cannot afford a judgment," LeBow said. "We're not Philip Morris. We're not RJR (RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp ).
"We can't afford to post a bond or an appeal or pay these huge legal fees. ... There are obviously business reasons to reach a settlement," LeBow said.
